column1: # The read path over a file this boot wrote (`KNOWN_ISSUES.md` item 60).
# A file's eighth and later blocks live behind its single-indirect block, and an
# indirect entry `write_map` has not filled yet is a zero, not `0xFFFFFFFF`. When
# that zero was read as a *valid* block number, a runtime-written file's blocks 8
# onward all resolved to block 0: the writes landed on the boot block and every
# read returned whichever of them was written last. A file of seven blocks or
# fewer never showed it, which is why the earlier coreutils steps did not.
# `filereadprobe` is the reader because no other tool can say what one read of a
# chosen size got: `od` reads 16 bytes at a time, `md5sum` reads the whole file,
# and both hide which layer was wrong. The sums are FNV-1a 64 of the bytes read,
# computed from `seq 1 10000`'s known output (48894 bytes), so a wrong block shows
# as a wrong number rather than as another hash to compare.
# `seq 1 10000` is 48894 bytes: twelve blocks, so blocks 0-6 are direct, block 7
# is indirect entry 0, and blocks 8-11 are the entries a fresh indirect block
# leaves zeroed.
coreutils seq 1 10000 > /fr1
coreutils wc -c /fr1
filereadprobe /fr1 0 48894 0
column2: filereadprobe: pos=0 off=0 len=48894 chunk=0 got=48894 sum=3d86a12d29c1503a first=310a320a330a340a

column1: # The same bytes one block at a time: the size of a read must not matter.
filereadprobe /fr1 0 48894 4096
